newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM'S REMARKS RAISE SPECTRE OF WORKING POOR
The Prime Minister's call for consideration of a minimum wage to attack unemployment has been condemned by the Federal Opposition and the ACTU.
Mr Howard is arguing that setting a low minimum wage will stimulate employment.
He says countries like America have chosen to follow such a path, and have reduced unemployment.
Mr Howard says Australia has always believed that if you get work, you ought to be paid a higher minimum wage than in the United States.
He says there needs to be more flexibility in the labour market, within the Australian ethos.
But Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says setting low minimum wages will hurt low paid people.
Mr Beazley says it would create more insecurity for families on low incomes, and would stifle economic growth.
The ACTU agrees, saying Mr Howard's proposal would import the American problem of the working poor.
It has accused the Prime Minister of attempting to blame low paid workers for high unemployment levels.
ACTU Assistant Secretary, Greg Combet, says Mr Howard's argument is intellectually deficient, and would make life more difficult for the low paid.
"It's quite clear what he's suggesting the debate should be about. "When they talk about flexibility on wage levels, they don't mean flexibility up, they mean flexibility down," Mr Combet says.

"John Howard is just searching for some excuse for their inability to do something about unemployment... It wasn't long ago that migration levels were suggested to be contributing to unemployment, now we're going to blame low paid workers."
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry says the Industrial Commission should set a minimum wage as a single stand-alone safety net for workers.
MILITANT CORE TO BLAME FOR DANDENONG TROUBLE
Police at Dandenong, east of Melbourne, are blaming a militant minority for last night's ugly demonstration at a One Nation Party rally.
One man was attacked by three protesters after leaving the town hall.
He was taken to hospital suffering head injuries.
Police used video cameras to film the crowd, estimated at more than 1,000, and say 10 people will face charges over incidents including the throwing of rotten eggs and bottles.
Police Superintendent, Jim Hart, says people should be able to freely express their views.
Superintendent Hart says there is a core of people from a militant minority who usually cause the problems at such events.
US ACTIVIST THREATENS TO CALL BOYCOTT TO SYDNEY OLYMPICS
American civil rights activist, Lorenzo Ervin says he will call for a boycott of the Sydney Olympics if he is deported from Australia.
The former black panther says he expects to be taken into custody and deported after his closed meeting with immigration officials in Brisbane today.
Mr Ervin says he has no chance of a fair hearing and accused Prime Minister, John Howard, of double standards.
He says South African President, Nelson Mandela, was allowed into Australia despite having a criminal record.
Mr Ervin says there will be international condemnation if he is deported.
Mr Howard, says he is surprised Mr Ervin was allowed into Australia, considering the existence of a law which allows visitors to be rejected if they are of bad character.

"Now I would have thought somebody who's been convicted of plane hijacking and who is invited to this country to address a group of people who are declared anarchists is hardly somebody who qualifies as being of good character," Mr Howard says.
"I can't for the life of me understand how, if the proper procedures were followed, he was allowed in."
But Mr Ervin's solicitor, Terry Fisher, says there's no reason for Mr Ervin to be deported, based on a hijacking conviction from the 1960s.
"The interesting thing is that he's received an executive clemency under the Bush administration in 1988 in relation to the offences in 1969," Mr Fisher says.
NO GOVT ACTION ON HUNTER COAL STRIKE

In New South Wales, State Rail's Freight Corp has claimed there is an understanding between the Public Transport Union and the miners' union about the picket outside the Hunter Valley number one coal mine.
The Industrial Relations Commission has heard trains attempting to pass the picket have twice been turned back as they have attempted to load coal from the mine.
The Public Transport Union has rejected Freight Corp's claim and has also questioned the jurisdiction under which part of this afternoon's hearing has been called.
The commission has adjourned this afternoon's hearing into private conference between the parties.
Meanwhile, the State Government has ruled out any intervention in the strike.
The Opposition today urged the government to use what powers it has to get police to remove the picketers, who are blocking trains trying to load coal at the mine.
State Industrial Relations Minister, Jeff Shaw, says the focus must be on resolving the dispute in an amicable way, rather than talking about force or coercion.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
